{{Short description|Set of isolated points in the spectrum of an operator with finite-rank Riesz projectors}}

In mathematics, specifically in [[spectral theory]], a '''discrete spectrum''' of a [[closed linear operator]] is defined as the set of [[isolated point]]s of its spectrum such that the [[rank (linear algebra)|rank]] of the corresponding [[Riesz projector]] is finite.

The discrete spectrum can also be defined as the set of normal eigenvalues.

==Definition==
A point <math>\lambda\in\C</math>
in the [[Spectrum (functional analysis)|spectrum]] <math>\sigma(A)</math> of a [[Unbounded_operator#Closed_linear_operators|closed linear operator]] <math>A:\,\mathfrak{B}\to\mathfrak{B}</math> in the [[Banach space]] <math>\mathfrak{B}</math> with [[Unbounded_operator#Definitions_and_basic_properties|domain]] <math>\mathfrak{D}(A)\subset\mathfrak{B}</math> is said to belong to the ''discrete spectrum'' <math>\sigma_{\mathrm{d}}(A)</math> of <math>A</math> if the following two conditions are satisfied:<ref name="ReedSimonIV">{{ cite book
|author1=Reed, M.
|author2=Simon, B.
|title=Methods of modern mathematical physics, vol. IV. Analysis of operators
|year=1978
|publisher = Academic Press [Harcourt Brace Jovanovich Publishers], New York
}}
</ref>
# <math>\lambda</math> is an isolated point in <math>\sigma(A)</math>;
# The [[rank (linear algebra)|rank]] of the corresponding [[Riesz projector]] <math>P_\lambda=\frac{1}{2\pi\mathrm{i}}\oint_\Gamma(z I_{\mathfrak{B}} - A)^{-1}\,dz</math> is finite.

Here, <math>I_{\mathfrak{B}}</math> is the [[identity operator]] in the Banach space <math>\mathfrak{B}</math>, and <math>\Gamma\subset\C</math> is a [[Simple closed curve|simple closed]] counterclockwise-oriented curve bounding an open region <math>\Omega\subset\C</math> such that <math>\lambda</math> is the only point of the spectrum of <math>A</math> in the closure of <math>\Omega</math>; that is, <math>\sigma(A)\cap\overline{\Omega}=\{\lambda\}.</math>

== Normal eigenvalues ==
The set of points in the discrete spectrum is equal to the set of normal eigenvalues.<ref name="GohbergKrein1960">{{ cite journal
|author1=Gohberg, I. C
|author2=Kreĭn, M. G.
|title=Fundamental aspects of defect numbers, root numbers and indexes of linear operators
|journal=American Mathematical Society Translations
|volume=13
|year=1960
|pages=185–264
|doi=10.1090/trans2/013/08
|url=http://mi.mathnet.ru/umn7581
}}</ref><ref name="GohbergKrein1969">{{ cite book
|author1=Gohberg, I. C
|author2=Kreĭn, M. G.
|title=Introduction to the theory of linear nonselfadjoint operators
|year=1969
|publisher = American Mathematical Society, Providence, R.I.
|url=http://gen.lib.rus.ec/book/index.php?md5=9CE2F03854312C3E29ED684CD84D8CA3
}}
</ref><ref name="BoussaidComech2019">{{ cite book
|author1=Boussaid, N.
|author2=Comech, A.
|title=Nonlinear Dirac equation. Spectral stability of solitary waves
|year=2019
|publisher = American Mathematical Society, Providence, R.I.
|isbn=978-1-4704-4395-5
|url=https://bookstore.ams.org/surv-244
}}</ref>
:<math>\sigma_{\mathrm{d}}(A)=\{\mbox{normal eigenvalues of }A\}.</math>

===Root lineal===
Let <math>\mathfrak{B}</math> be a [[Banach space]]. Consider a [[Densely defined operator|partially defined]] linear operator <math>A:\,\mathfrak{B}\to\mathfrak{B}</math> with domain <math>\mathfrak{D}(A)</math>. The [[Generalized eigenvector#Root lineal of a linear operator in a Banach space|root lineal]] <math>\mathfrak{L}_\lambda(A)</math> corresponding to an eigenvalue <math>\lambda\in\sigma_p(A)</math> is defined as the set of elements <math>x</math> such that <math>x, (A-\lambda I_{\mathfrak{B}}) x, (A-\lambda I_{\mathfrak{B}})^2 x, \dots</math> all belong to <math>\mathfrak{D}(A)</math>, and that after finitely many steps, we end up with zero: <math>(A-\lambda I_{\mathfrak{B}})^k x = 0</math>.

This set is a [[linear manifold]] but is not necessarily closed. If it is closed (for example, when it is finite-dimensional), it is called the [[generalized eigenspace]] of <math>A</math> corresponding to the eigenvalue <math>\lambda</math>.

===Normal eigenvalue===
An [[eigenvalue]] <math>\lambda\in\sigma_p(A)</math> of a [[Unbounded_operator#Closed_linear_operators|closed linear operator]] <math>A:\,\mathfrak{B}\to\mathfrak{B}</math> in the [[Banach space]] <math>\mathfrak{B}</math> with [[Unbounded_operator#Definitions_and_basic_properties|domain]] <math>\mathfrak{D}(A)\subset\mathfrak{B}</math> is called '''normal''' (in the original terminology, ''<math>\lambda</math> corresponds to a normally splitting finite-dimensional root subspace'') if the following two conditions are satisfied:<ref name="GohbergKrein1957">{{ cite journal
|author1=Gohberg, I. C
|author2=Kreĭn, M. G.
|title=Основные положения о дефектных числах, корневых числах и индексах линейных операторов
|trans-title=Fundamental aspects of defect numbers, root numbers and indexes of linear operators
|journal=Uspekhi Mat. Nauk |series=New Series
|volume=12
|issue=2(74)
|year=1957
|pages=43–118
|url=http://mi.mathnet.ru/umn7581
|trans-journal=Amer. Math. Soc. Transl. (2)
}}</ref><ref name="GohbergKrein1960" /><ref name="GohbergKrein1969" />
# The [[algebraic multiplicity]] of  <math>\lambda</math> is finite: <math>\nu=\dim\mathfrak{L}_\lambda(A)<\infty</math>, where <math>\mathfrak{L}_\lambda(A)</math> is the root lineal of <math>A</math> corresponding to the eigenvalue <math>\lambda</math>;
# The space <math>\mathfrak{B}</math> can be decomposed into a [[direct sum]] <math>\mathfrak{B}=\mathfrak{L}_\lambda(A)\oplus \mathfrak{N}_\lambda</math>, where <math>\mathfrak{N}_\lambda</math> is an [[invariant subspace]] of <math>A</math> in which <math>A-\lambda I_{\mathfrak{B}}</math> has a bounded inverse.

===Equivalent characterizations===

{{Math theorem
| name = Equivalent characterizations
| note = <ref name="BoussaidComech2019" />{{Reference page|location=Theorem III.88}}
| math_statement = Let <math>A:\,\mathfrak{B}\to\mathfrak{B}</math> be a closed linear [[densely defined operator]] in the Banach space <math>\mathfrak{B}</math>, then the following are equivalent:

# <math>\lambda\in\sigma(A)</math> is a normal eigenvalue;
# <math>\lambda\in\sigma(A)</math> is an isolated point in <math>\sigma(A)</math> and <math>A-\lambda I_{\mathfrak{B}}</math> is [[Fredholm operator#semi-Fredholm operators|semi-Fredholm]];
# <math>\lambda\in\sigma(A)</math> is an isolated point in <math>\sigma(A)</math> and <math>A-\lambda I_{\mathfrak{B}}</math> is [[Fredholm operator|Fredholm]];
# <math>\lambda\in\sigma(A)</math> is an isolated point in <math>\sigma(A)</math> and <math>A-\lambda I_{\mathfrak{B}}</math> is [[Fredholm operator|Fredholm]] of index zero;
# <math>\lambda\in\sigma(A)</math> is an isolated point in <math>\sigma(A)</math> and the rank of the corresponding [[Riesz projector]] <math>P_\lambda</math> is finite;
# <math>\lambda\in\sigma(A)</math> is an isolated point in <math>\sigma(A)</math>, its algebraic multiplicity <math>\nu=\dim\mathfrak{L}_\lambda(A)</math> is finite, and the range of <math>A-\lambda I_{\mathfrak{B}}</math> is [[Closed range theorem|closed]].<ref name="GohbergKrein1957" /><ref name="GohbergKrein1960" /><ref name="GohbergKrein1969" />

In all such cases, the root lineal <math>\mathfrak{L}_\lambda(A)</math> is closed, and equals the range of the Riesz projector.<ref name="GohbergKrein1969" />
}}

==Relation to other spectra==

=== Isolated eigenvalues of finite algebraic multiplicity ===
In general, the rank of the Riesz projector can be larger than the dimension of the [[Generalized eigenvector#Root lineal of a linear operator in a Banach space|root lineal]] <math>\mathfrak{L}_\lambda</math> of the corresponding eigenvalue, and in particular it is possible to have <math>\mathrm{dim}\,\mathfrak{L}_\lambda<\infty</math>, <math>\mathrm{rank}\,P_\lambda=\infty</math>. So, there is the following inclusion:

: <math>\sigma_{\mathrm{d}}(A)\subset\{\mbox{isolated points of the spectrum of }A\mbox{ with finite algebraic multiplicity}\}.</math>

In particular, for a [[Nilpotent operator|quasinilpotent operator]]

: <math>Q:\,l^2(\N)\to l^2(\N),\qquad Q:\,(a_1,a_2,a_3,\dots)\mapsto (0,a_1/2,a_2/2^2,a_3/2^3,\dots),</math>

one has <math>\mathfrak{L}_\lambda(Q)=\{0\}</math>, <math>\mathrm{rank}\,P_\lambda=\infty</math>.
Therefore, <math>\lambda=0</math> is an isolated eigenvalue of finite algebraic multiplicity, but it is not in the discrete spectrum:
<math>\sigma(Q)=\{0\}</math>,
<math>\sigma_{\mathrm{d}}(Q)=\emptyset</math>.

=== Point spectrum ===
The discrete spectrum <math>\sigma_{\mathrm{d}}(A)</math> of an operator <math>A</math> is not to be confused with the [[point spectrum]] <math>\sigma_{\mathrm{p}}(A)</math>, which is defined as the set of [[eigenvalue|eigenvalues]] of <math>A</math>. Each point of the discrete spectrum is an eigenvalue, so
:<math>\sigma_{\mathrm{d}}(A)\subset\sigma_{\mathrm{p}}(A).</math>
However, they may be unequal. An eigenvalue may not be an isolated point of the spectrum, or it may be isolated, but with an infinite-rank Riesz projector. For example, for the ''left shift operator'',
<math>
L:\,l^2(\N)\to l^2(\N),
\quad
L:\,(a_1,a_2,a_3,\dots)\mapsto (a_2,a_3,a_4,\dots),
</math>
the point spectrum is the open unit disc <math>\mathbb{D}_1</math> in the [[complex plane]], the full spectrum is the closed unit disc <math>\overline{\mathbb{D}_1}</math>, and the discrete spectrum is empty:
:<math>\sigma_{\mathrm{p}}(L)=\mathbb{D}_1,
\qquad
\sigma(L)=\overline{\mathbb{D}_1},
\qquad
\sigma_{\mathrm{d}}(L)=\emptyset.
</math>
This is because <math>\sigma_{\mathrm{p}}(L)</math> has no isolated points.

=== Spectral decomposition ===
The spectrum of a closed operator <math>A:\,\mathfrak{B}\to\mathfrak{B}</math> in a Banach space <math>\mathfrak{B}</math> can be decomposed into the union of two [[disjoint sets]]: the discrete spectrum and the fifth type of the [[essential spectrum]] (see page for the definition of each type):
:<math>
\sigma(A)= \sigma_{\mathrm{d}}(A)\cup\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}, 5}(A).
</math>
